description: We combine systems architecture, product thinking, AI, research and communication to turn complex satellite radar into something anyone can explore and trust.
summary:
EARTH//PULSE is a calamity-awareness solution that uses NASA Earth observation data, including NISAR radar, to give people simple, local early warnings for any place on Earth.

Natural disasters such as floods, droughts, wildfires, landslides and glacier hazards usually show early signs in satellite data before they strike. NASA records these signs every day, but the data is spread across technical websites that most people never use. As a result, the warnings often don’t reach the people who need them most.

EARTH//PULSE solves this by bringing the data together into one easy-to-read card. The card explains in plain language whether a hazard is building up nearby, and shows which NASA source each piece of information comes from.

The card also changes depending on who is using it. Families can check the risk around their home. Farmers can set their own limits for rain, dry spells, heat and frost, and get alerts when those limits are crossed. Climbers can see the conditions at the altitude they plan to reach.

Behind every card, NISAR radar from NASA and ISRO can see through clouds and darkness. By comparing radar passes over the same place, it reveals flooding and ground movement that ordinary satellite photos can miss.

With EARTH//PULSE, people can learn about danger earlier, make better decisions and protect their lives and livelihoods, using free and trusted NASA science.
details:
EARTH//PULSE: Watch Earth Change

Every day, NASA satellites record rainfall, soil moisture, heat, fire and ground movement across the entire planet. Most of that knowledge never reaches the farmer watching the sky or the climber planning an ascent. EARTH//PULSE closes that gap. It turns NASA Earth observations, including NISAR radar, into one clear local card for any place on Earth, with the NASA source behind every claim.

What It Does

Users choose a location by searching, using their current position or selecting one of 24 continuously watched cities. They then choose a persona. In seconds, EARTH//PULSE delivers a single card:

  • A plain-language headline with a colour-coded level (All Clear, Watch or Warning), such as “74 active fires within 50 km” or “Saturated ground and 50 mm more rain this week.”
  • The alerts behind the headline, each traced to its NASA source.
  • A 7-day forecast strip, openly labelled as the app’s only non-NASA input.
  • NASA evidence tiles: 7- and 30-day rainfall against the 2001–2025 normal, surface soil wetness against normal, temperature anomaly, active fires within 50 and 150 km, open natural events, landslide history within 50 km, and the most recent NISAR radar pass overhead.

Built Around People, Not Dashboards

The same NASA data means different things to different lives, so EARTH//PULSE frames it around the people who use it:

  • Farmer: Farmers set their own limits for heavy rainfall, dry-spell length, heat and frost, which are saved on their device. EARTH//PULSE alerts them when NASA observations or the forecast cross those limits, showing when the season’s rain turns from helpful to harmful, or when a dry spell becomes a drought.
  • Climber: Climbers enter a target altitude and see the estimated freezing level and temperature at that height. They also get snow-depth change, the local landslide record, and direct links to NASA’s glacial-lake inventory and the LHASA landslide nowcast.

Going Deeper

A single tap opens the full exploration tool:

  • 19 NASA data layers on an interactive 3D globe with a 14-day time-lapse
  • Live NASA FIRMS fire detections and NASA EONET natural events
  • A NISAR change engine: click any place, and it finds two real radar passes and computes a surface-change map directly in the browser
  • Five NISAR case studies: Bangladesh monsoon floods, the Kumamoto M6.8 earthquake, Punjab crops, Rondônia forest clearing and the Greenland ice sheet

How It Works

A single server endpoint per place (/api/pulse) brings together five NASA sources:

  • NASA POWER: daily rainfall, temperature, surface soil wetness, snow depth and elevation, each compared with that location’s own 2001–2025 normal
  • NASA FIRMS: active fire detections
  • NASA EONET: ongoing natural events
  • NASA Global Landslide Catalog: historical landslide records
  • ASF DAAC: the latest NISAR radar passes

These inputs feed a transparent Hazard Signal Index, which scores rain surplus, rain deficit, soil saturation, heat anomaly, fire density and nearby events. Every formula is shown inside the app. The index measures observed signals. It is not a prediction, and the app says so plainly.

Every data point shows where it came from. Each item carries a data class and a freshness status (Live, Cached, Archived or Unavailable). When data is missing, EARTH//PULSE says so. It never fills the gap with simulated values.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Early warning where it matters: vulnerable communities receive local warning signals that conventional weather apps miss.
  • Better decisions in the field: farmers can protect crops and plan around damaging rain or emerging drought.
  • Safer mountains: climbers and mountain communities can see the warm, wet conditions that come before glacier collapses and glacial-lake outburst floods.
  • Science made everyday: advanced NASA data that is usually hard to reach becomes a simple daily habit.

What’s next: push alerts for phones and smartwatches, local-language support, and calibrated NISAR flood measurements through an Earthdata-authenticated worker.

Tools and Technologies

  • Application: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, Vite, CesiumJS for the 3D globe, satellite.js for SGP4 orbit propagation, and a Node.js API that caches every upstream data source
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy and Pillow
  • Video production: HyperFrames with GSAP and FFmpeg
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, helped write code, text and the project film. ElevenLabs generated the voiceover. Both are fully declared in the project and the video description.

What Makes It Creative

  • One dataset, many lives: persona cards reframe the same NASA data for home, field and mountain instead of offering one generic dashboard.
  • Your sky, not a stock image: the home screen shows yesterday’s real NASA satellite image of the user’s own region.
  • Radar as proof: NISAR is not a separate demo. It is the evidence layer behind every card.

What We Considered

  • Honesty: measured, derived and modelled items are clearly labelled, the index states that it is not a forecast, and NISAR products are marked as provisional.
  • NASA first: the weather forecast is the only non-NASA input, and it is labelled as such.
  • Performance: heavy map layers load only when the globe is opened, so the card stays fast on mobile networks.
  • Accessibility: plain language, readable type and layouts designed to work at phone width.

EARTH//PULSE makes NASA science useful in daily life, for the people who need it most.
